anchors.fact: An importer launched the Amaretto Sour in 1974 as amaretto and lemon juice, two to one. By the 1980s it was a standard drink, and most bartenders made it with bought sour mix. (F1–F2; Oxford pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: A drink everyone had stopped thinking about: the decision was made, and nobody argued.
anchors.speaksTo: fear: Powerlessness (the decision made before anyone could think)

anchors.fact: The Oxford entry calls that version flat: an easy drink that tasted of little but the liqueur. (F3; pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: The scorn had a point, and the case for the drink starts by saying so.

anchors.fact: On 9 February 2012 a Portland bartender, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, posted on his own website that he made the best Amaretto Sour in the world. It opens "No, really. I'm serious." (F6; post 2012)
anchors.meaning: The side nobody was on, taken on purpose, in public, and funny.
anchors.speaksTo: essence: spark debate and provoke controversy · tone: provocative

anchors.fact: The post agrees with the critics first: the usual ones are too sweet, and amaretto alone is too weak to hold its own. A sour has to be adjusted for this liqueur, he wrote, and his answer to the weakness is cask-proof bourbon. (F7; post 2012)
anchors.meaning: He argued for the thing by granting everything true that was said against it.

anchors.fact: Some readers ribbed him in the comments. One asked whether it was still an Amaretto Sour with bourbon in it, and another said he wouldn't call it one. (F9; post comments, 10–21 Feb 2012)
anchors.meaning: The price: a ribbing and the purist's question. Never "resented".
anchors.speaksTo: fear: being written off as contrary

anchors.fact: One reader remembered the old ones as "sickly sweet", and another, a bartender, wrote that he'd make it to restore public faith in amaretto. (F11; post comments, 2012)
anchors.meaning: The scorn he argued against, on the same page.
anchors.speaksTo: the room that had stopped thinking

anchors.fact: By 2021, the Oxford Companion's entry on the Amaretto Sour was his. It grants the old version's flatness and says the drink "can be greatly improved": lemon juice again, a little egg white, cask-strength bourbon. (F4–F5; pdf 97)
anchors.meaning: The argument became part of the drink's own record, won or lost. Told plainly: he wrote the entry.
anchors.speaksTo: goal: Liberation (a mark left) · driver: Leave a mark

anchors.fact: The *Cocktail Codex* (Death & Co's team) prints the Amaretto Sour among its classics: fresh lemon, less syrup, no bourbon or egg. (F13; *Codex* p. 114)
anchors.meaning: Another bar's book treats it as a classic. Never "his version became the classic".
anchors.speaksTo: what they give: the idea holds up

anchors.fact: Jim Meehan's Oxford entry on variations gives the bourbon added to an Amaretto Sour at a Portland bar, Pépé Le Moko, as an example of a bar's own deliberate twist. (F14; pdf 533; his bar per pdf 2269)
anchors.meaning: His addition is known to others by name. Never "a new standard" (that sentence is general).

anchors.fact: In 2014 he titled another post "Hot Toddies suck—long live the Hot Toddy". What Oxford takes from it is his way to keep a toddy hot, not just warm. (F16; Oxford TODDY pdf 2034, 2036)
anchors.meaning: The same move from the other side: knocked in the title, fixed in the body. Never "attacked the drink everyone loves" (the post is unread).
anchors.speaksTo: the one true thing: argues against what might be true

anchors.fact: Our glass follows his 2012 post for the amaretto (45 ml), cask-strength bourbon (22.5 ml), egg white, old-fashioned glass, fresh ice and lemon peel. The syrup is out, the lemon is cut from 30 to 22.5 ml and half a teaspoon of sherry vinegar is in: all three are ours. His own two printings differ on the syrup (15 ml simple vs 5 ml 2:1). (F4, F8, C1)
anchors.meaning: Ours, built on his fix. Never "his recipe" or "made his way".

cocktail.closingLine: Measure the vinegar, and be ready to defend it. Next time, let the view you defend be one you hold.
method: Fill the glass with fresh ice and leave it to chill.
Separate a fresh egg. Whip the white with a fork for about 20 seconds, until it's loose and frothy, then measure one tablespoon. You won't need the rest.
Pour the amaretto, bourbon, lemon juice and sherry vinegar into a shaker. Add the spoonful of egg white last.
Fill the shaker with ice, close it, and shake hard for about 15 seconds.
Strain into the glass, over the fresh ice. A thin white foam will settle on top.
Squeeze the lemon peel over the foam, shiny side down, so its oils fall on the drink, then lay it on top.
cocktail.name: Hear Me Out

recipe.note: bottled at or near barrel strength; 55% or stronger
the Spanish kind (vinagre de Jerez); measure it, don't guess
from a fresh egg; whip the white, then measure a spoonful

cocktail.tagline: You'll argue the other side. Sometimes it's even yours.

reading.epigraph: One bartender made the case for this drink by admitting what was wrong with it.
whoYouAre: Someone says it's settled, and something in you sits up. It isn't that you think they're wrong. Often you think they're right. But nobody has argued with it yet, and an idea nobody has argued with hasn't been tested. It's only been agreed with. So you take the other side.

You'd hardly ever admit how often you agree, or how glad you'd be to lose to a good answer. "Only playing devil's advocate" keeps your own view safe, where nobody can argue it down. The sigh is what you dread, the "there they go again": once your questions stop counting, you're stuck with decisions nobody was allowed to think about.

Nobody says thank you in the moment. They should. An idea that's survived you can survive almost anything, and when the real objection comes, from a boss, say, the others already have the answer, because you made them find it.
yours: In the 1980s the Amaretto Sour was a standard. An importer had launched it in 1974 as two parts of the sweet Italian liqueur to one of lemon juice, but by then most bartenders reached for bought sour mix instead, and the drink tasted of little but the liqueur.

Then, in February 2012, a Portland bartender, Jeffrey Morgenthaler, posted on his website that he made the best Amaretto Sour in the world. It opens: "No, really. I'm serious." And before he made his case, he gave the other side its due. Other Amaretto Sours were too sweet, he wrote, and amaretto on its own is weak. "It needs help." His help was cask-strength bourbon. Some readers teased him, and one asked whether it was still an Amaretto Sour at all.

That's the move I recognise in you. He never pretended the old drink was good. He granted the point, then showed what the drink could be once it was answered. Two years later he tried the move from the other end, with a post called "Hot Toddies suck—long live the Hot Toddy", and a better way to keep one hot. And by 2021, the entry on the Amaretto Sour in the *Oxford Companion to Spirits and Cocktails* was his. I like to think the teasing pleased him: it meant someone was arguing back.

The cocktail I've made for you is an Amaretto Sour, a classic again, built on his fix: an Italian amaretto, cask-strength bourbon for backbone, fresh lemon, and lightly whipped egg white, a spoonful of it, shaken and strained over fresh ice, with lemon oil over its thin white foam. Then I argued with him, as you would. He said the others were too sweet, so I took him further than he went: no syrup at all, a little less lemon to match, and the amaretto doing all the sweetening. And there's sherry vinegar in it, half a teaspoon, an ingredient I'd have to defend in most bars, in honour of the side nobody takes. Vinegar is one of the best partners nuts have in the kitchen, and here it keeps the sweetness honest.

Here's my side, and I mean it. Keep testing everything: people are better for it, even the ones who sigh. But now and then, argue for something you actually love, and say plainly that it's what you think. No escape hatch, no "just for the sake of argument". Let them push back on you for a change. You may find your own ideas survive you too, and everyone else finally gets to argue with the real you.
